title: Project files, language version, and auto-imports
hook: Every modern C# app has a small XML project file that tells the build system which .NET version to target and which C# syntax to allow. Pin your settings to the target framework — not to "latest" — so every machine builds the same way.

blocks.text: An SDK-style project file (.csproj) is the build contract for your app. It declares the Software Development Kit (SDK) to use, the Target Framework Moniker (TFM) like net10.0, and optional settings such as LangVersion and ImplicitUsings. The TFM picks the default C# language version — .NET 10 maps to C# 14. You rarely need to set LangVersion manually; the pairing is designed to stay in sync.

entries.plainDefinition: A string like net10.0 that tells the build which .NET runtime and API surface your app targets.
A project setting that controls which C# syntax features the compiler accepts.
entries.example: net10.0 defaults to C# 14; you can override with <LangVersion>14.0</LangVersion>.

entries.plainDefinition: A project setting that auto-generates global using statements for common namespaces like System and System.Linq.
entries.example: With ImplicitUsings enabled, Console.WriteLine works without writing using System;.

blocks.text: Reproducible builds depend on pinned settings. Setting LangVersion to latest means "whatever compiler is installed" — two Continuous Integration (CI) agents can accept different syntax and fail unpredictably. The TFM also gates which runtime APIs exist: raising LangVersion without raising TFM leads to code that compiles but cannot find runtime types. Implicit usings reduce boilerplate in apps but can hide dependencies in libraries where you want every namespace visible in source.

blocks.title: Default rule
blocks.body: Let the TFM choose the language version. Override LangVersion only when you have a deliberate reason, and never use latest in shared or production projects.

items.title: SDK attribute selects the build SDK
items.body: <Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk"> pulls in default compile, test, and publish targets.

items.title: TFM selects runtime + default LangVersion
items.body: net10.0 implies C# 14 and .NET 10 Base Class Library (BCL) APIs.

items.title: Implicit usings inject global imports
items.body: The build generates a GlobalUsings.cs with namespaces like System, System.Collections.Generic, and System.Threading.Tasks.

items.title: Roslyn compiles with the resolved settings
items.body: You can verify the actual pair with #error version in any .cs file.

snippet.label: Recommended SDK-style project
snippet.explanation: net10.0 plus the current SDK already compiles as C# 14. No LangVersion line needed. Nullable enable turns on null-safety annotations.

snippet.label: Wrong vs right LangVersion
snippet.code:
<!-- Wrong: machine-dependent syntax -->
<LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>

<!-- Right: explicit only when you mean it -->
<LangVersion>14.0</LangVersion>
snippet.explanation: latest tracks the installed compiler, not a stable language version. Two build agents with different SDKs can disagree on what compiles.

snippet.explanation: A quick way to see what Roslyn resolved for your project. Remove or comment out before shipping.

blocks.title: Project config parallels
rows: TFM selects runtime APIs and default language version
No direct equivalent (TS target is looser)
C# LangVersion gates syntax features tightly
Auto-imports namespaces already in referenced assemblies

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Raising LangVersion without raising TFM, then hitting missing runtime APIs. Thinking implicit usings replace NuGet references — they only import namespaces from assemblies you already reference. Copy-pasting Directory.Build.props LangVersion across C# and Visual Basic projects — the version numbers are not interchangeable between languages.

interviewTakeaways: Default language version follows the target framework; .NET 10 maps to C# 14.
`LangVersion=latest` is a reproducibility smell; prefer TFM or an explicit major like `14.0`.
Implicit usings are generated global usings, not magic scope.
commonPitfalls: Raising LangVersion without raising TFM, then hitting missing runtime APIs.
Thinking implicit usings replace NuGet references — they only import namespaces already referenced by the SDK.
Copy-pasting `Directory.Build.props` LangVersion across C# and VB projects — the version numbers are not the same language.

jsTsCorrelations.note: compilerOptions.target and lib are closer to TFM than to LangVersion. Using latest in tsconfig has the same "depends which tsc" risk as LangVersion=latest.
